output:
Student A: Basketball Hobbyist Routine

Goal and intensity
- Objective: Have fun, stay active, improve core skills to enjoy rec or school team play.
- Intensity: Moderate (RPE 5–6). Sessions feel challenging but conversational; avoid excessive fatigue.
- Weekly volume: 3 training days (60–75 minutes each) + 1 optional day of pickup/cross-training.

Weekly structure
- Day 1: Skills + light conditioning
  - Warm-up (5–8 min): Jog, high knees, butt kicks, dynamic stretches, ankle hops.
  - Ball handling (10 min): Stationary crossover/behind-the-back/in-and-out; pound dribbles; figure-8; eyes up.
  - Shooting form (20 min): 50 close-range form shots (hold follow-through); 5 spots x 10 makes midrange; free throws 20 attempts.
  - Finishing (10 min): 30 layups each side; inside hand and off-foot finishes; add a cone to simulate defender.
  - Defense (8–10 min): Stance, slides, closeouts to a coach’s point; 3 sets x 20–30 seconds.
  - Small-sided game (15–20 min): 2-on-2 or 3-on-3 with constraints (e.g., must use weak hand once per possession).
  - Cool-down (5 min): Light stretching hips, calves, quads.

- Day 2: Footwork, passing, agility
  - Warm-up (5–8 min).
  - Footwork (10 min): Jump stops, front/rear pivots, stride stops; add “catch-turn-shoot” on command.
  - Passing circuits (15 min): Wall or partner passing (chest, bounce, overhead) 3 x 20 reps; target accuracy.
  - Shooting variety (20 min): Catch-and-shoot from 5 spots x 8 makes; one-dribble pull-ups both directions x 10 each; 20 free throws.
  - Agility (10 min): Cone shuffles, zig-zag slides, ladder work; 4 x 20–30 seconds, moderate effort.
  - Fun challenge (10–15 min): HORSE or knockout.

- Day 3: Game IQ + free throws + conditioning
  - Warm-up (5–8 min).
  - Ball-handling moves (10 min): Hesitation, cross, inside-out into layup; 3 sets each side.
  - Free-throw routine (15 min): 30 attempts with consistent breathing and dribble count; track percentage.
  - Simple team concepts (10 min): Give-and-go, backdoor cut timing, screen and pop; walk-through pace, then half-speed.
  - Defensive closeouts (10 min): Shot/drive read; two-hand contest; don’t fly by.
  - Conditioning (8–10 min): Jump rope or court intervals (half-court down and back x 10 at moderate pace).
  - Cool-down (5 min).

Optional activity
- 1 day pickup game or cross-training (30–60 min): Soccer, swimming, biking, or casual game play.

Strength and mobility (2x/week, 15–25 min)
- Bodyweight and band work: Squats, lunges, push-ups, band rows, glute bridges, calf raises, planks/side planks (2–3 sets of 10–15).
- Mobility: Hip flexors, hamstrings, ankles, thoracic spine.

Progress markers (every 4 weeks)
- Free throws: Aim for 60–70% in practice.
- Left-hand layups: Make 20 in a row without missing.
- Shooting: 50 makes from midrange in ≤15 minutes.
- Ball-handling: Complete a cone dribble course cleanly both hands.

Safety and recovery
- 1–2 full rest days weekly; sleep 8 hours.
- Hydrate; wear supportive shoes; stop if pain (especially knee/ankle).
- Keep sessions fun; rotate drills to avoid boredom and overuse.


Student B: Aspiring Professional Routine

Goal and intensity
- Objective: Build elite skill, athleticism, game IQ, and durability for college/pro pathway.
- Intensity: High, varied by day (RPE 7–9). Prioritize quality reps, clear metrics, and recovery.
- Weekly volume: 6 training days (10–14 hours total) with 1 full rest day. Periodize across the year.

Sample weekly plan
- Monday
  - AM Skill/Shooting (75–90 min): 50 form shots; 5 spots x 20 makes catch-and-shoot; 5 spots x 12 off-the-dribble; relocation threes; 100 free throws (target ≥85–90%).
  - PM Lower Strength + Plyos (60 min): Trap-bar deadlift or front squat 4 x 4–6; split squats 3 x 6–8; RDL 3 x 6–8; box jumps 4 x 3; med-ball chest and scoop throws 4 x 6; core carries.

- Tuesday
  - AM Skill/Finishing + PnR reads (75 min): Euro/pro hop/inside hand/reverse—20–30 reps each side; floater series; 2-on-1, 3-on-2 decision drills; pocket/skip passes.
  - PM Conditioning + Agility (45–60 min): Repeated sprint ability (10 x baseline-to-baseline, 30–40 sec rest); 5–10–5 shuttle practice; lane agility; Film study (30 min): own clips and a pro comp at your position.

- Wednesday
  - AM Shooting under fatigue (75–90 min): Drift/hammer actions; “5-in-a-row” ladder; contested closeout shooting; 100 free throws.
  - PM Upper Strength + Core (60 min): DB bench 4 x 6–8; pull-ups/rows 4 x 6–10; face pulls, cuff external rotations 3 x 12–15; Pallof press/ab wheel; suitcase carries.

- Thursday
  - Recovery + Mobility (45 min): Foam roll; hips/ankles/T-spine; isometric adductor/hamstring work; breathing drills.
  - Light Skill (45 min): Form refinement, one-dribble pull-ups, finishing touch shots; Film/mental (30 min): scout tendencies, visualization.

- Friday
  - AM Game Situations (75–90 min): Live 1v1/2v2/3v3 constraints (e.g., 0.5 decisions, must hit roller once per set); shell defense; closeouts with shot/drive read.
  - PM Lower Power + Speed (60 min): Contrast sets (light jump then squat); 10–20 m sprints (6–8 reps, full rest); lateral shuffle/crossover steps; rim touches.

- Saturday
  - Mixed Play and Shooting Challenge (60–90 min): Controlled scrimmage; 300–400 total makes from varied actions; free-throw pressure sets (10 x 10 with ≥90% or restart).
  - Prehab (20 min): Knee/ankle stability (eccentric calf, tibialis raises, single-leg balance); glute med activation.

- Sunday
  - Full rest: No structured training; light walk/stretch only.

Technical focus blocks
- Shooting volume target: 500–800 made shots per week; track makes, spots, and percentages.
- Ball handling: Two-ball series, pace changes, pickup/gather; 10–15 min daily.
- Passing and reads: Pocket, hook, skip, “one more”; 0.5-second decision-making; add defenders to force reads.
- Defense: Stance/angles, closeouts, help-recover, screen navigation; 1v1 containment; rebounding/box-outs.

Performance benchmarks (adjust for position and training age)
- Speed: 3/4-court sprint ≤3.2 s; 5–10–5 shuttle ≤4.5 s.
- Agility: Lane agility competitive for HS elite; measure monthly.
- Power: Standing vertical 28–32+ inches; approach vertical higher.
- Conditioning: Yo-Yo or beep test improving monthly; repeated sprint drop-off ≤7%.
- Strength (under supervision): Trap-bar deadlift 1.5x BW; front squat 1.25x BW; 8+ strict pull-ups; stable single-leg strength.

Recovery and nutrition
- Sleep: 8–9 hours nightly; consistent schedule.
- Fuel: Pre-session carbs + protein; post-session 20–30 g protein + carbs within 60 minutes; hydrate with electrolytes.
- Soft tissue/mobility daily (10–15 min); deload week every 6–8 weeks or after heavy competitive blocks.
- Monitor wellness: RPE, soreness, and HRV or morning resting HR; adjust volume if recovery lags.

Safety and support
- Lift with qualified coaching; prioritize technique before load.
- Progress loads and volumes gradually; avoid year-round maximal plyo volumes.
- Keep a training log (shots, lifts, sprints, wellness scores); review weekly with coach.
- Integrate film and mental skills: 2–3 takeaways per week, visualization before games.

How to choose and stick to the right routine
- If basketball is mainly for enjoyment and social play, follow Student A’s moderate plan and keep the variety high.
- If your goal is college/pro, follow Student B’s plan, track metrics, and periodize intensity around school and season.

Feeling overwhelmed? Meditation offers a simple, science-backed way to unwind your nervous system and build resilience to daily stress. By training attention and cultivating nonjudgmental awareness, even short, regular sessions can shift your body from fight-or-flight into rest-and-digest.

Benefits at a glance:
- Reduces physiological stress markers like cortisol
- Calms the sympathetic nervous system, boosting parasympathetic tone and heart rate variability
- Improves emotion regulation and reduces rumination
- Enhances focus and working memory, aiding productivity
- Supports better sleep quality
- Lowers blood pressure over time
- Builds resilience, compassion, and well-being

Evidence: A meta-analysis of 47 randomized trials found mindfulness meditation programs produced moderate improvements in anxiety and psychological stress (Goyal et al., JAMA Internal Medicine, 2014). Other research reports decreased cortisol and improved autonomic balance after brief training in integrative body–mind techniques (Tang et al., Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 2007).

Getting started is easy. Choose a quiet spot, sit comfortably, and set a timer for 5–10 minutes. Focus on the sensation of breathing. When the mind wanders, gently note it and return to the breath without judgment. Practice daily; consistency matters more than duration. Over weeks, you’ll feel calmer, clearer, and in control.

Course concept
- Title: Modern World History, 1500–Present (16-week high school course)
- Big goals: Build historical thinking skills; analyze change and continuity; compare societies; evaluate causes and consequences; read and source primary documents; write evidence-based arguments; connect past to present.
- Essential questions (examples): How do ideas, technology, and power shape global change? What drives revolution and reform? How do empires rise, rule, and fall? How do individuals and movements influence historical trajectories?

Curriculum development process (backward design)
1) Identify standards and competencies
- Align to your state social studies standards and the C3 Framework (Developing Questions, Applying Disciplinary Tools, Evaluating Sources, Communicating Conclusions, Taking Informed Action).
- Emphasize skills: sourcing, corroboration, contextualization, argumentation, data literacy, map literacy, public speaking.

2) Define summative assessments and grading
- Two midterm exams (Weeks 6 and 11) and a cumulative final exam (Week 16).
- Major performance tasks: DBQ essay, comparative case study paper, oral history interview product, group “virtual museum exhibit.”
- Ongoing formative work: weekly source analyses, short quizzes, class activities, participation.

3) Sequence content and set weekly objectives
- Organize conceptually and chronologically across four units: Early Modern World (1500–1750), Revolutions and Industry (1750–1900), War and Upheaval (1900–1950), Cold War to Globalization (1950–Present).
- For each week, define 3–5 measurable objectives tied to skills and content.

4) Design assignments and learning experiences
- Pair each week’s objectives with aligned activities, readings, and deliverables.
- Scaffold writing (claims, evidence, reasoning) and document skills throughout.
- Schedule major tasks so they build toward exams and reduce end-of-term overload.

5) Select diverse resources
- Mix primary sources, maps, data sets, short documentaries, podcasts, museum artifacts, and scholarly overviews.
- Provide multiple access points (text, audio, visuals) and choices for student voice.

6) Plan differentiation and supports
- Include graphic organizers, sentence frames, guided notes, chunked readings, audio versions, vocabulary supports, enrichment options, and alternative formats for performance tasks.

7) Build rubrics and feedback routines
- Use transparent criteria for each task; provide models and exemplars; incorporate self/peer review and revision cycles.

8) Monitor and adjust
- Use exit tickets, quick writes, and quiz data to adjust pacing and reteach. Gather student feedback mid-semester and revise as needed.

Assessment and grading breakdown (100% total)
- Participation and in-class activities: 10%
- Short assignments and quizzes (weekly source analyses, map/vocab/data quizzes): 20%
- DBQ essay (major paper): 12%
- Comparative case study paper: 8%
- Oral history interview product (audio, transcript, or mini-podcast plus analysis): 10%
- Group project: Virtual museum exhibit (curated digital exhibit with narrative): 15%
- Midterm Exam 1 (Week 6): 10%
- Midterm Exam 2 (Week 11): 10%
- Final Exam (Week 16): 15%

Week-by-week plan: objectives, activities, resources, assignments
Week 1: Introduction to historical thinking and the early modern world
- Objectives: Practice sourcing/corroboration; interpret maps; establish classroom norms; set personal goals.
- Activities: Source detective station rotation; “What is a reliable source?” mini-lesson; world regions map workshop; baseline skill diagnostic.
- Resources: Stanford History Education Group lesson; World Digital Library; Google Earth.
- Assignments: Learning log setup; short reflection on historical thinking; diagnostic not graded (feedback only).

Week 2: Renaissance, Reformation, and print cultures
- Objectives: Explain how ideas and technology influence belief systems and power; analyze humanist and reform texts.
- Activities: Jigsaw on Erasmus/Luther/Calvin; printing press simulation; gallery walk of art/pamphlets.
- Resources: Project Gutenberg excerpts; British Museum images; Crash Course videos (selected segments).
- Assignments: Map quiz (regions and trade routes); Source Analysis 1 (annotate two short primary sources with sourcing questions).

Week 3: Global exchanges and the Columbian Exchange
- Objectives: Evaluate ecological and demographic impacts; assess indigenous perspectives; use maps/data to track change.
- Activities: Columbian Exchange mapping lab; fishbowl on perspectives of conquest; commodity case studies (silver, sugar).
- Resources: Our World in Data charts; NAAM slave trade database; Indigenous accounts (Bartolomé de las Casas, Nahua sources).
- Assignments: Source Analysis 2; Short comparison paragraph on two regions’ exchange impacts.

Week 4: States and empires (Ottoman, Mughal, Qing; mercantilism)
- Objectives: Compare governance and religious policies; analyze imperial legitimation; discuss mercantilism’s effects.
- Activities: Role-play advisors crafting reform memos; primary-source stations (firmans/edicts); comparative charting.
- Resources: Smithsonian Asian Art; Ottoman archives (translated); economic diagrams.
- Assignments: Comparative Case Study proposal (choose two polities with a focus question).

Week 5: Enlightenment and Atlantic revolutions
- Objectives: Connect Enlightenment ideas to political change; source revolutionary documents.
- Activities: Socratic seminar on Locke/Rousseau; DBQ mini-lab with excerpt sets (US, French, Haitian).
- Resources: Avalon Project (declarations); Haitian Constitution selections.
- Assignments: Source Analysis 3; Draft thesis and outline for Comparative Case Study; DBQ mini practice paragraph.

Week 6: Midterm Exam 1 + Industrial Revolution foundations
- Objectives: Demonstrate Unit 1–2 understanding; identify causes of industrialization and regional variations.
- Activities: Review game (Jeopardy); midterm exam; intro mini-lecture and artifact analysis (spinning jenny, steam engine).
- Resources: Museum of Science & Industry images; factory records.
- Assignments: Midterm 1; Comparative Case Study paper due (1200–1500 words).

Week 7: Industrialization’s social and environmental impacts
- Objectives: Interpret factory accounts; analyze labor movements; assess environmental change.
- Activities: Factory report simulation; source comparison (employers vs. workers); “design a reform bill.”
- Resources: Sadler Report; photographs; air quality maps; selected Dickens excerpts.
- Assignments: Source Analysis 4; Quiz on industrial terms; short data commentary (graph).

Week 8: Nationalism, imperialism, and resistance (c. 1850–1914)
- Objectives: Explain motives and methods of imperialism; contrast resistance movements; evaluate Meiji reforms.
- Activities: Scramble for Africa negotiation simulation; jigsaw of resistance case studies (India, Ethiopia, Vietnam).
- Resources: Berlin Conference docs; Meiji Charter Oath; maps.
- Assignments: Source Analysis 5; Group project kickoff (team selection, topic proposal, artifact list).

Week 9: World War I and its aftermath
- Objectives: Analyze causes; interpret propaganda; connect war aims to peace settlements.
- Activities: Propaganda gallery walk; trench warfare tech demo; treaty mapping activity.
- Resources: National Archives posters; Treaty of Versailles clauses; casualty data.
- Assignments: Source Analysis 6; DBQ mini on WWI causes; Quiz (WWI terms/events).

Week 10: Interwar years: economic crisis and authoritarianism
- Objectives: Explain links between the Great Depression and political change; compare regimes; examine culture/arts.
- Activities: Timeline build; case study stations (Italy, Germany, USSR); art analysis (Dada, propaganda).
- Resources: IMF/World Bank historical data; speeches; art collections.
- Assignments: Source Analysis 7; Finalize museum exhibit storyboard; short annotated bibliography (5 sources).

Week 11: World War II, genocide, and global conflict
- Objectives: Assess causes and turning points; define and examine genocide; analyze home-front mobilization.
- Activities: Map-based campaign analysis; survivor testimony (age-appropriate excerpts); ethical sourcing lesson.
- Resources: USHMM primary sources (non-graphic); PBS Frontline clips; Pacific theater archives.
- Assignments: Midterm Exam 2; Museum exhibit draft submitted for feedback.

Week 12: Decolonization and the early Cold War
- Objectives: Compare independence movements; explain Cold War origins; evaluate formation of the UN.
- Activities: Debate on nonalignment; source set on partition and independence; UN charter analysis.
- Resources: UN Charter; speeches (Nkrumah, Nehru); maps of new states.
- Assignments: DBQ Essay prompt released; Source Analysis 8; DBQ draft thesis and document table.

Week 13: Cold War transformations and social movements
- Objectives: Explain containment and détente; connect civil rights and global movements; analyze media.
- Activities: Fishbowl on 1968; Cuban Missile Crisis decision-making simulation; media literacy mini-lesson.
- Resources: JFK tapes (transcripts); protest posters; radio/podcast clips.
- Assignments: DBQ Essay due (1500–1800 words); Quiz (Cold War terms); Oral history planning (topic, consent form, questions).

Week 14: Globalization, technology, environment
- Objectives: Use data to analyze globalization; evaluate environmental policies; discuss digital revolution impacts.
- Activities: Data walk (trade, inequality, emissions); policy brief workshop; tech timeline.
- Resources: Gapminder; Our World in Data; climate agreements; WTO materials.
- Assignments: Infographic or data brief (student choice); Oral history interview conducted.

Week 15: Contemporary conflicts, migration, and human rights
- Objectives: Explain causes of regional conflicts; analyze migration patterns; evaluate human rights frameworks.
- Activities: Model UN mini-session; student-curated museum exhibit presentations; peer reviews.
- Resources: UNHCR maps; human rights case files; news literacy guide.
- Assignments: Museum exhibit final due; Oral history product due (audio/transcript plus 600–800 word analysis); Portfolio reflection draft.

Week 16: Synthesis and final exam
- Objectives: Synthesize course themes; demonstrate cumulative skills; reflect on learning.
- Activities: Concept mapping; final review stations; final exam; course feedback forms.
- Resources: Student portfolios; review packets.
- Assignments: Final Exam; Portfolio reflection due (500–700 words).

Major assignments: descriptions and criteria
- Short assignments and quizzes (20%)
  - Weekly source analyses: Students annotate 1–2 primary sources using sourcing prompts (author, context, purpose, audience), identify claims/evidence, and write a 150–250 word analysis. Eight submissions across Weeks 2–12.
  - Quizzes: Four short quizzes on maps/terms/data (Weeks 2, 7, 9/10, 13). Mixed formats (matching, map labeling, short responses).
  - Grading criteria: Accuracy and completeness; correct use of evidence; sourcing; clarity and mechanics; submitted on time.

- DBQ Essay (12%)
  - Task: 1500–1800 word essay responding to a prompt (Week 12 release; due Week 13) using 8–10 provided documents plus 2 teacher-approved outside sources.
  - Criteria (typical breakdown): Clear thesis and sustained argument; use of documents with accurate evidence extraction; sourcing (POV, purpose, historical context, audience) and corroboration; contextualization and complexity (counterclaims, connections); organization and mechanics.

- Comparative Case Study Paper (8%)
  - Task: 1200–1500 word comparative analysis (due Week 6) comparing two polities/empires on a focused theme (e.g., taxation, religious policy, military organization).
  - Criteria: Focused comparative framework; precise evidence from at least 4 primary sources and scholarly summaries; analysis of similarities/differences and causes; clear organization; citations.

- Oral History Interview Product (10%)
  - Task: Conduct an interview with a community member about a lived experience connected to course themes (e.g., migration, Cold War, civil rights). Produce either a 6–8 minute edited audio with show notes or a cleaned transcript plus a 600–800 word analytical commentary tying the narrative to historical context.
  - Criteria: Preparation and ethical practice (consent, respectful questioning); technical quality or transcript quality; depth and relevance of questions; analytical commentary linking to sources; reflection on limitations.

- Group Virtual Museum Exhibit (15%)
  - Task: In teams of 3–4, curate a digital exhibit (e.g., Google Sites/Adobe Express/Canva) with 8–12 artifacts (images, maps, documents, short clips), captions, and an overarching narrative on a selected theme (e.g., “Resistance and Reform, 1850–1950”).
  - Criteria: Historical accuracy; purposeful selection and curation of diverse sources; narrative coherence and design; analytical captions with sourcing; collaboration (peer evaluation); presentation quality.

Exams: formats and criteria
- Midterm Exam 1 (10%, Week 6)
  - Coverage: Weeks 1–5.
  - Format: 25 multiple choice (skills and content), 2 short-answer prompts (sourcing/contextualization), 1 mini-DBQ (4–5 docs, 1–2 paragraph response).
  - Criteria: Content understanding; skill application; clear, concise written responses.

- Midterm Exam 2 (10%, Week 11)
  - Coverage: Weeks 6–10.
  - Format: 25 multiple choice, 2 short-answer prompts, 1 mini-DBQ.
  - Criteria: Same as above, with emphasis on cause/effect and comparison.

- Final Exam (15%, Week 16)
  - Coverage: Cumulative, with emphasis on synthesis across Units 3–4.
  - Format: 30 multiple choice, 3 short-answer prompts, 1 document-based essay (shorter than the major DBQ; 800–1000 words) or thematic essay (teacher’s choice).
  - Criteria: Synthesis of themes; evidence use; argumentation; accuracy and clarity.

Classroom activities to boost engagement
- Station rotations: Primary source detective work; map/data interpretation; artifact captioning.
- Role-plays and simulations: Berlin Conference, Paris Peace Conference, Cuban Missile Crisis, Model UN.
- Socratic seminars and fishbowl discussions: Structured protocols with assigned roles (summarizer, evidence finder, counter-arguer).
- Gallery walks: Student-curated visuals with “thinking routine” prompts (See-Think-Wonder).
- Jigsaw readings: Expert groups teach each other subtopics.
- Debate formats: Policy debates on imperialism, industrial reforms, decolonization strategies.
- Think-pair-share and quick writes: Frequent low-stakes processing to check understanding.
- Student choice: Options for products (infographic, brief, podcast, video) on select weeks.
- Local history tie-ins: Connect global themes to community artifacts, immigration stories, civic institutions.

Diverse resources (curate age-appropriate excerpts)
- Primary sources: World Digital Library; Library of Congress; National Archives; British Museum online; USHMM (non-graphic testimonies); EuroDocs.
- Skill-building: Stanford History Education Group lessons; Facing History and Ourselves; Zinn Education Project (use judiciously with multiple perspectives).
- Multimedia: Crash Course (selected episodes); BBC/PBS documentaries (clips); NPR’s Throughline; Google Arts & Culture virtual tours.
- Data/maps: Gapminder, Our World in Data, UN Data; historical atlases; Google Earth.
- Reference/background: OpenStax World History; reputable encyclopedia entries for overview reading.
- Note: Pre-screen content for sensitivity (genocide, war); provide content warnings and alternative materials as needed.

Differentiation and supports
- Provide guided notes and graphic organizers; tiered readings (primary-source excerpts at multiple complexity levels); audio versions and text-to-speech access.
- Vocabulary supports: Frayer models, word walls, bilingual glossaries.
- Writing scaffolds: Claim-evidence-reasoning frames; sentence starters; outline templates; exemplar paragraphs.
- Assessment flexibility: Choice of product formats (written/audio/video) with common criteria; extended time per IEP/504; small-group testing; chunked deadlines.
- Extension options: Additional sources, deeper data analysis, historiography mini-essays for advanced learners.

Feedback and course evaluation
- Weekly exit tickets to spot misconceptions.
- Mid-semester survey to adjust pacing/resources.
- Draft-review cycles for major tasks (peer review with protocols).
- Transparent rubrics shared in advance and used during self-assessment.
- End-of-course reflection linking growth in specific skills (sourcing, argumentation, data literacy) to artifacts in a portfolio.

Implementation notes
- Pacing: Adjust based on school calendar (holidays/testing). Weeks with exams include lighter homework.
- Academic integrity: Teach citation basics (MLA/Chicago), paraphrasing, and proper use of AI tools if applicable.
- Accessibility: Ensure digital content meets accessibility standards; provide printed copies on request.
- Community partnerships: Consider inviting a local historian or arranging a virtual museum visit.

This plan gives you a clear development process, week-by-week objectives, aligned assignments and exams, detailed grading criteria, and a toolkit of engaging activities and diverse resources to create a dynamic, equitable Modern World History course.

output:
We are Earthbound, a movement for conservation and sustainability anchored in justice, science, and solidarity. The crisis is urgent, but solvable. We choose action over despair, repair over extraction, and collective wellbeing over short-term profit.

Our goals are concrete and time-bound. Cut greenhouse gas emissions by fifty percent by 2030 and achieve net-zero well before 2050. Protect and restore nature: conserve thirty percent of land and seas by 2030, connect wildlife corridors, reforest degraded hillsides, and revive wetlands and rivers. Transition to clean energy: deliver carbon-free electricity by 2040, phase out coal by 2030, electrify transport and buildings, and prioritize efficiency and demand response. Build a circular economy: halve waste by 2030, ban unnecessary single-use plastics, design for repair, reuse, and recycling, and make producers responsible for end-of-life. Secure clean air and water with strong standards, PFAS phase-outs, modernized wastewater treatment, and nature-based solutions. Transform food systems by scaling regenerative agriculture and agroforestry, protecting soils, halving food waste, supporting plant-rich diets, and ensuring fair, safe farm labor. Align money with life: end fossil subsidies by 2028, require climate risk disclosure, mobilize public green finance, divest from extractive industries, and invest locally. Advance environmental justice by centering frontline and Indigenous communities, guaranteeing meaningful consent, and sharing data openly. Grow resilient cities with efficient transit, safe biking and walking, urban forests, cool roofs, and deep retrofits for healthy homes.

We will achieve this through public policy, community power, and everyday choices. We will vote, organize, and hold leaders accountable. We will retrofit buildings, install solar, plant native trees, compost, conserve water, and buy repairable, regional goods. We will mentor green workers, build cooperatives, and open-source solutions. We will measure progress with transparent dashboards and annual audits.

Join us. Protect what protects us. Build prosperity that regenerates. Act together, now. For future generations.

Etta: She wraps bowls in newspapers from Finch Grocery, saved for decades. Water licks porch steps; she hums recipes. Her husband left during spring flood, never returned. She names spices like children, pockets the battered whisk. When the siren starts, Etta locks memory in drawers and chooses the boat. Today.

Kieran: The county engineer presses the red button he argued for at meetings. His father taught him water's patience beside the willow. He knows head height of every resident from survey notes. Watching houses detach into boats, Kieran whispers sorry to maps, folds guilt neatly, then activates the gates. alone.

Mei: Third-grade teacher, she labels boxes by reading level. The blue mailbox outside her classroom holds promise notes from kids—drawings of fish, boats, future jobs. Mei tucks her own letter inside: I’m scared, but I will learn again. When the siren wails, she carries chalk like prayer. In her pocket.

Luis: He grew up mending nets on the porch, listening for the church bell's hour. Now he ratchets trailer hitches, helps neighbors launch their lives. Carp flicker through streets like rumors. He ties one last knot—bowline, reliable—and stops pretending he won’t miss the willow. He drives toward new water. anyway.

Avani: In Finch’s back room, she tends the seed library—labels smudged with years. Her grandmother carried marigolds across continents; Avani carries them across water. She hangs bouquets upside down, saves the lives that fit in envelopes. Tomorrow, she’ll plant by the new shore, counting petals like prayers, forgiving the river.

Jonas: Caretaker of Saint Brigid’s, he oils the church bell, whispers apologies to bronze. He planned to lift it out; water came sooner, heavier. In the attic, he stacks hymnals like sandbags, pets the old dog. When the bell tolls underwater tomorrow, Jonas will hear it only in bones. forever.

Salma: Seventeen, she livestreams the siren so distant friends can hear the valley’s throat close. She paints her lips marigold; blames Avani. Her mother says pack, pack, pack. Salma hides love notes in the blue mailbox, plays guitar until strings rust with rain, scrapes song into her phone. for memory.

Dmitri: Years later, he dives Lake Brigid for lost things. He follows carp past rooftops, measures silt depth like time. A whisk gleams in a kitchen window; he pockets it, imagines a woman naming spices. The bell is silent. Dmitri surfaces into wind, returns small metal to shore. for Etta.

Noor: Born after the flood, she brings coffee to fishermen, poetry to the shoreline. She reads soggy letters in the museum—children promising futures. Dmitri left a whisk here labeled Etta. Noor believes naming saves things. At sunset, the lake glows; willow’s drowned crown flickers. Noor whispers, We kept you. safe.

Former National Football League player, actor, and broadcaster O.J. Simpson was tried for two accounts of murder in 1994. Simpson was accused of murdering his ex-wife Nicole Brown Simpson and a restaurant waiter, Ron Goldman.

Simpson was represented by a high-profile defense team, that many referred to as the Dream Team. It included famous names like Robert Shapiro, Johnnie Cochran, and Robert Kardashian.

Cochran was able to convince the jury that there was reasonable doubt about the DNA evidence, and he alleged misconduct by the Los Angeles Police Department.

However, the families of the deceased filed a civil lawsuit against Simpson. The jury unanimously found him guilty for both deaths, and awarded the families $33.5 million for compensatory and punitive damages.

Many feel the justice system prevailed 13 years later when Simpson was convicted and sentenced on robbery and weapons charges.

instruction: Write a short essay comparing Western and Eastern cultures. Your essay should be organized into five paragraphs, each exploring a different perspective on the cultures. For each paragraph, follow this structure: the first sentence should introduce the perspective being compared, the second sentence should describe the aspect of Western culture relevant to that perspective, the third sentence should describe the corresponding aspect of Eastern culture, and the fourth sentence should highlight the key differences or similarities between the two.
decomposed_questions: Is the generated text a short essay that compares Western and Eastern cultures?

Does the third sentence of each paragraph describe the corresponding aspect of Eastern culture?
Does the fourth sentence of each paragraph highlight the key differences or similarities between the two cultures?
output:
A foundational perspective, acknowledging regional diversity, is the conception of self and community. In many Western settings, the self is framed as autonomous, with personal rights, self-expression, and individual achievement seen as moral goods. Across many Eastern traditions, the self is understood as relational, with filial duty, role obligations, and social harmony guiding behavior. Thus the axis tilts toward individual goals in the West and collective responsibilities in the East, even as both prize dignity, belonging, and mutual care.

Another useful perspective is communication style and the expression of meaning. Western cultures often favor low-context, direct speech that prizes clarity, explicit argument, and comfort with constructive disagreement. Eastern cultures more often use high-context, indirect cues that emphasize nuance, face-saving, and attunement to relationship and setting. The difference lies in explicitness and confrontation norms, yet both aim to convey respect and shared understanding in social exchange.

A third perspective concerns time orientation and approaches to planning. Western practice typically treats time as linear and segmented, elevating punctuality, deadlines, and measurable efficiency. Eastern practice often couples formal punctuality with a cyclical, long-horizon outlook, privileging patience, endurance, and process to sustain relationships and outcomes. Accordingly, the West skews task- and clock-centered while the East leans relationship- and horizon-centered, though both rely on schedules to coordinate complexity.

Education and learning philosophy offer a fourth perspective. Western models commonly encourage inquiry, debate, and learner agency, using discussion and experimentation to cultivate critical thinking. Eastern models often stress disciplined practice, respect for teachers, and exam-focused mastery, building depth through repetition and perseverance. The contrast is pedagogical—dialogic exploration versus structured mastery—yet both value excellence and increasingly blend these approaches.

Finally, views of authority and leadership provide a fifth perspective. Western institutions tend to idealize low power distance, transparency, and flatter hierarchies, with leaders cast as facilitators accountable to rules and rights. Eastern institutions more often accept higher power distance and seniority, with leaders as stewards who broker harmony and build consensus through gradual alignment. The key difference is comfort with hierarchy and the path to consensus—open contestation versus discreet alignment—though effective leadership in both rests on competence and responsibility.

Let t be time in seconds. With frequency f = 5 Hz, angular frequency ω = 2πf = 10π rad/s, amplitude A = 2, and period T = 1/f = 0.2 s:

a) Sine wave: x(t) = 2 sin(10π t)

b) Square wave (symmetric, ±2): x(t) = 2 sgn(sin(10π t))

instruction: Explain the basics of chemical bonding, including ionic, covalent, and metallic bonds. output:
- Ionic bonds: Formed when one atom transfers electrons to another, creating oppositely charged ions that stick together by electrostatic attraction. Typically occurs between a metal (which loses electrons) and a nonmetal (which gains them). These compounds often form hard crystals, have high melting points, and many dissolve in water. Examples: NaCl (table salt, where sodium gives one electron to chlorine) and MgO (magnesium gives two electrons to oxygen).

- Covalent bonds: Formed when two nonmetal atoms share pairs of electrons to reach a more stable arrangement. The shared electrons hold the atoms together in molecules. Covalent bonds can be single, double, or triple, and sharing can be equal (nonpolar) or unequal (polar). Examples: H2O (water, polar covalent bonds between hydrogen and oxygen) and O2 (oxygen gas, a double bond with equal sharing between the two oxygen atoms).

- Metallic bonds: Found in pure metals and alloys. Metal atoms release some of their electrons, which become free to move throughout the solid like a “sea” of electrons. These mobile electrons glue the metal ions together and explain metals’ properties: good electrical and heat conductivity, malleability, and ductility. Examples: Cu (copper, used in electrical wires) and Al (aluminum, used in foil and frames).

        # Input layer -> first hidden layer
        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(input_dim, hidden_dim1)
        # ReLU activation for the first hidden layer
        self.relu1 = nn.ReLU()

        # First hidden layer -> second hidden layer
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(hidden_dim1, hidden_dim2)
        # ReLU activation for the second hidden layer
        self.relu2 = nn.ReLU()

        # Second hidden layer -> output layer
        self.fc3 = nn.Linear(hidden_dim2, output_dim)

    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        # Pass through input layer to first hidden layer and apply ReLU
        x = self.fc1(x)
        x = self.relu1(x)

        # Pass through first hidden to second hidden layer and apply ReLU
        x = self.fc2(x)
        x = self.relu2(x)

        # Pass through the output layer (typically logits for classification)
        x = self.fc3(x)
        return x

# Example usage: instantiate the model and run a forward pass
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Assume inputs are 100-dimensional and we want 10 output units (e.g., classes)
    model = TwoHiddenFFN(input_dim=100, hidden_dim1=64, hidden_dim2=128, output_dim=10)

    # Create a sample batch of 32 examples with 100 features each
    sample_input = torch.randn(32, 100)

    # Compute the outputs
    outputs = model(sample_input)

    # The output shape should be [batch_size, output_dim] -> [32, 10]
    print("Output shape:", outputs.shape)

output: "One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman." Beauvoir's insight foregrounded the social construction of gender and exposed how patriarchal norms shape femininity. Yet its historical frame - binary, Eurocentric, largely cis-heterosexual and middle-class - limits its reach today. The category "woman" is no longer presumed stable: trans, nonbinary, and intersex experiences complicate the idea that gender is solely a product of socialization into a feminine role, as many assert an intrinsic identity that resists or precedes such norms. Intersectionality reveals how race, class, colonial histories, disability, and religion contour gendered life in ways underemphasized in Beauvoir's analysis; there is no universal path of "becoming." Contemporary legal gains, reproductive technologies, and digital cultures also diversify agency, allowing resistance and self-definition beyond the domestic and workplace scripts she critiqued. While her claim still illuminates how power molds gender, applying it unmodified risks flattening plural realities and reinscribing a Western binary. Today, "becoming" is manifold, contested, and self-directed, not only the effect of patriarchal conditioning.

Earth may feel solid under your feet, but it’s actually a planet that’s always moving—very slowly. The ground we live on is part of giant slabs of rock called tectonic plates. Understanding how these plates move helps explain why earthquakes shake the ground and why volcanoes erupt.

What are tectonic plates?
- Earth is made of layers. The outer, rigid layer is called the lithosphere. It includes the crust (where we live) and the very top of the mantle. The lithosphere is broken into pieces called plates.
- Beneath the plates is a softer, hotter layer called the asthenosphere. It can flow slowly, a bit like very thick taffy. The plates “float” on this moving layer.
- Think of Earth’s outer shell like a cracked eggshell or a jigsaw puzzle. Each piece is a plate, and the cracks between them are plate boundaries.

What makes plates move?
- Heat from deep inside Earth causes slow currents in the mantle (convection). These currents drag plates along.
- Plates are also pushed from mid-ocean ridges where new crust forms (ridge push) and pulled down where older, heavier plates sink back into the mantle (slab pull).
- The motion is slow—usually as fast as your fingernails grow—but over millions of years it reshapes the planet.

Types of plate boundaries and what they do
- Divergent boundaries: Plates move apart.
  - Where it happens: Mid-ocean ridges (like the Mid-Atlantic Ridge) and rift zones on land (like the East African Rift).
  - What you see: New crust forms as magma rises and cools. There are frequent, usually smaller earthquakes and volcanoes that often produce runny, basalt lava.
- Convergent boundaries: Plates move toward each other.
  - Oceanic plate meets continental plate: The denser oceanic plate sinks (subducts) into the mantle. This creates deep ocean trenches, strong earthquakes, and chains of volcanoes on the continent (like the Andes or the Cascades).
  - Oceanic plate meets oceanic plate: One subducts beneath the other, forming volcanic island arcs (like Japan).
  - Continental plate meets continental plate: Neither plate easily sinks, so they crumple and push up huge mountains (like the Himalaya). These zones have powerful earthquakes but few or no volcanoes.
- Transform boundaries: Plates slide past each other sideways.
  - Where it happens: The San Andreas Fault in California is a famous example.
  - What you see: Frequent earthquakes. Because plates aren’t diving or pulling apart here, volcanoes are rare along transform faults.

How plate motion causes earthquakes
- Plates don’t slide smoothly. Their edges can lock due to friction. Stress builds up as the plates try to move.
- When the stress becomes too great, the rocks suddenly break or slip along a fault, releasing energy as seismic waves. That shaking is an earthquake.
- Many of the strongest earthquakes happen at convergent boundaries, especially where one plate dives under another (megathrust earthquakes). Transform boundaries can also produce damaging quakes.

How plate motion causes volcanoes
- Magma forms when parts of the mantle melt. Plates help this happen in a few ways:
  - At divergent boundaries, the mantle rises and pressure drops, causing melting (decompression melting). This makes basaltic magma that can flow easily.
  - At subduction zones, water and other materials carried down by the sinking plate help the mantle melt (flux melting). This magma can be thicker and gassier, leading to more explosive eruptions.
- Volcanoes away from boundaries: Some volcanoes form above hotspots, where extra-hot mantle plumes rise from deep within Earth. As a plate moves over a hotspot, it can create a chain of volcanoes, like the Hawaiian Islands. This is why not all volcanoes sit on plate boundaries.

The Ring of Fire and other big patterns
- The Pacific “Ring of Fire” is a horseshoe-shaped zone with many subduction zones around the Pacific Ocean. It has most of the world’s earthquakes and many active volcanoes.
- Mid-ocean ridges circle the globe under the seas, constantly creating new ocean floor.
- Plate tectonics also builds mountains, opens and closes oceans, and, in rare cases, triggers tsunamis when big undersea earthquakes suddenly move the seafloor.

Putting it all together
- Earth’s plates are always on the move because of heat inside the planet.
- Where plates meet, we get most earthquakes and many volcanoes.
- The type of boundary—divergent, convergent, or transform—helps predict whether we’ll see volcanoes, earthquakes, mountains, or all of the above.
- Some volcanoes form far from boundaries at hotspots, and a few earthquakes happen within plates, but plate edges are where the action usually is.

Quiz

Multiple Choice (choose one answer)
1) Earth’s tectonic plates are part of which layer?
A. Inner core
B. Lithosphere
C. Asthenosphere
D. Outer core
Answer: B. Lithosphere

2) Which type of boundary most often creates strong earthquakes and chains of volcanoes because one plate sinks under another?
A. Divergent
B. Convergent
C. Transform
D. None of the above
Answer: B. Convergent

3) Why do volcanoes commonly form at subduction zones?
A. Friction directly turns rock into magma
B. Water from the sinking plate helps the mantle melt
C. Sunlight heats the crust until it melts
D. Gravity squeezes magma out of rocks
Answer: B. Water from the sinking plate helps the mantle melt

True or False
4) Most earthquakes happen on or near plate boundaries.
Answer: True

5) All volcanoes are found at plate boundaries.
Answer: False (hotspots like Hawaii are away from plate boundaries)

Overview:
- Purpose: A closed-loop transport network that delivers oxygen and nutrients to tissues, removes carbon dioxide and wastes, carries hormones, and supports temperature and pH balance.
- Heart: Central four-chamber pump. Right side sends deoxygenated blood to the lungs; left side sends oxygenated blood to the body. Valves keep blood moving one way.
- Blood vessels: Arteries carry blood away from the heart under pressure; veins return blood to the heart and serve as reservoirs; capillaries are thin exchange sites where gases, nutrients, and wastes move between blood and tissues.
- Lungs (pulmonary circulation): Oxygenate blood and remove carbon dioxide.
- Systemic circulation: Distributes oxygenated blood to organs and tissues and returns deoxygenated blood to the heart; includes coronary vessels that supply the heart muscle.
- Blood: Red blood cells carry oxygen; plasma transports nutrients, hormones, and wastes; platelets and clotting proteins stop bleeding; white blood cells support immunity.

Flowchart (blood flow direction):
Left ventricle -> Aorta/systemic arteries -> Tissue capillaries -> Systemic veins -> Right atrium -> Right ventricle -> Pulmonary arteries -> Lungs -> Pulmonary veins -> Left atrium -> Left ventricle

instruction: Please create concise and well-structured lecture notes on Quantum Mechanics, focusing on the following two topics: Schrödinger Equation, and Dirac Equation. For each topic, provide several bullet points with brief explanations and include at least one relevant equation. To ensure the equation are easy to read, use LaTeX code to format them.

output:
Schrödinger Equation
- Role and scope: Governs the time evolution of nonrelativistic quantum states ψ(x,t). Observables correspond to Hermitian operators acting on ψ.
- Time-dependent form (general Hamiltonian Ĥ):
  \[
  i\hbar\,\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\,\psi(\mathbf{x},t)=\hat{H}\,\psi(\mathbf{x},t)
  \]
  For a single particle in a potential V(x,t), 
  \[
  \hat{H}=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\nabla^2+V(\mathbf{x},t).
  \]
- Stationary states and energy eigenvalue problem (time-independent potential):
  \[
  \hat{H}\,\phi_n(\mathbf{x})=E_n\,\phi_n(\mathbf{x}),\quad \psi_n(\mathbf{x},t)=\phi_n(\mathbf{x})\,e^{-iE_n t/\hbar}.
  \]
- Probability density and current; continuity equation ensures conservation of probability:
  \[
  \rho(\mathbf{x},t)=|\psi|^2,\quad \mathbf{j}(\mathbf{x},t)=\frac{\hbar}{2mi}\left(\psi^*\nabla\psi-\psi\,\nabla\psi^*\right),
  \]
  \[
  \frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t}+\nabla\cdot\mathbf{j}=0.
  \]
- Operator formalism: Expectation values
  \[
  \langle \hat{A}\rangle(t)=\int \psi^*(\mathbf{x},t)\,\hat{A}\,\psi(\mathbf{x},t)\,d^3x,
  \]
  with canonical commutator
  \[
  [\hat{x}_i,\hat{p}_j]=i\hbar\,\delta_{ij}.
  \]
- Unitary time evolution (time-independent Ĥ): 
  \[
  \psi(t)=e^{-i\hat{H}t/\hbar}\,\psi(0).
  \]
- Boundary conditions and quantization: Normalizable solutions satisfy ∫|ψ|^2 d^3x=1; boundary conditions yield discrete spectra (e.g., particle in a box).
- Example (harmonic oscillator energies): 
  \[
  E_n=\hbar\omega\left(n+\frac{1}{2}\right),\quad n=0,1,2,\dots
  \]

Dirac Equation
- Motivation: Relativistic wave equation for spin-1/2 particles that is first-order in time and space, reproducing E^2=p^2c^2+m^2c^4 and introducing intrinsic spin.
- Covariant (free) form with gamma matrices:
  \[
  \left(i\hbar c\,\gamma^\mu \partial_\mu - m c^2\right)\psi(x)=0,
  \]
  where the gamma matrices satisfy the Clifford algebra
  \[
  \{\gamma^\mu,\gamma^\nu\}=2\eta^{\mu\nu}\,I_4,\quad \eta^{\mu\nu}=\mathrm{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1).
  \]
- Hamiltonian (free) form with 4-component spinor ψ:
  \[
  i\hbar\,\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\psi=\left(c\,\boldsymbol{\alpha}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{p}}+\beta\,m c^2\right)\psi,\quad \boldsymbol{\alpha}=\gamma^0\boldsymbol{\gamma},\ \beta=\gamma^0.
  \]
- Minimal coupling to electromagnetism (charge q):
  \[
  \left(i\hbar c\,\gamma^\mu D_\mu - m c^2\right)\psi=0,\quad D_\mu=\partial_\mu+\frac{i q}{\hbar c}A_\mu,
  \]
  or in Hamiltonian form
  \[
  \hat{H}=c\,\boldsymbol{\alpha}\cdot\left(\hat{\mathbf{p}}-q\mathbf{A}\right)+\beta\,m c^2+q\phi.
  \]
- Conserved 4-current and probability density:
  \[
  j^\mu=\bar{\psi}\gamma^\mu\psi,\quad \bar{\psi}=\psi^\dagger\gamma^0,\quad \partial_\mu j^\mu=0,\quad j^0=\psi^\dagger\psi\ge 0.
  \]
- Plane-wave solutions and energy spectrum (free particle):
  \[
  \psi(x)=u_s(\mathbf{p})\,e^{-ip\cdot x/\hbar},\quad E=\pm\sqrt{p^2 c^2+m^2 c^4},
  \]
  with four spinor states (two particle, two antiparticle).
- Spin and magnetic moment; nonrelativistic limit reproduces Pauli equation with g≈2:
  \[
  \hat{H}_{\text{Pauli}}\approx \frac{(\hat{\mathbf{p}}-q\mathbf{A})^2}{2m}+q\phi-\frac{q\hbar}{2m}\,\boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot\mathbf{B}.
  \]
- Antiparticles: Negative-energy solutions imply existence of antiparticles (e.g., positron); charge conjugation maps ψ→ψ^c.
- Chiral/massless limit: For m=0, the Dirac equation splits into two decoupled Weyl equations for left- and right-handed components.
- Discrete symmetries: Invariance properties under parity (P), charge conjugation (C), and time reversal (T) underpin CPT symmetry in relativistic quantum theory.

Equation: v^2 = u^2 + 2 a s (constant-acceleration kinematics)

Variables and units:
- v: final speed, in meters per second (m/s)
- u: initial speed, in meters per second (m/s)
- a: acceleration, in meters per second squared (m/s^2)
- s: displacement, in meters (m)

Given values:
- u = 5.0 m/s
- a = 2.00 m/s^2
- s = 20.0 m

Calculation:

- v = √(105 m^2/s^2) = 10.247 m/s ≈ 10.25 m/s

Result:
- v ≈ 10.25 m/s

Page 1
Non-Disclosure Agreement (NDA) for Software Development Project

This NDA is between Party A and Party B (each a Party) for discussing, evaluating, and performing a software development project (the Purpose).

Definitions:
- Confidential Information: non-public information disclosed by a Party, in any form, that is marked confidential or reasonably understood as confidential, including source code, designs, documentation, algorithms, roadmaps, test data, business plans, financials, customer/vendor data, pricing, and derivatives.
- Disclosure: any act by which a Party makes Confidential Information available to the other, including oral, written, visual, electronic, demonstrations, or system/repository access.
- Recipient: the Party receiving Confidential Information, including its directors, employees, contractors, advisors, and affiliates who access it only to further the Purpose and who are bound by obligations at least as protective as this NDA.
- Disclosing Party: the Party that makes a Disclosure of Confidential Information.

Recipient obligations:
- Use Confidential Information solely for the Purpose.
- Limit access to need-to-know and protect using no less than reasonable care.
- Do not copy, reverse engineer, decompile, or create derivatives except as necessary for the Purpose.
- Do not disclose to third parties without prior written consent.

Duration: These obligations remain in force for five (5) years from the last Disclosure under this NDA.
-----
Page 2
Return or destruction:
Upon request by the Disclosing Party or termination of discussions or the project, the Recipient will, within ten (10) business days, cease use; return or destroy all Confidential Information and materials containing it; and provide written certification. Electronic records must be securely deleted; removal from backups may occur through routine archival cycles, with continued protection and no use. One archival copy may be retained if required by law or compliance, subject to this NDA.

Exceptions:
Obligations do not apply to information that: (a) is or becomes public without Recipient’s breach; (b) was lawfully known to Recipient before Disclosure; (c) is independently developed without use of Confidential Information; (d) is received from a third party without duty of confidentiality; or (e) must be disclosed to comply with law, regulation, or court order. For compelled disclosures, Recipient will give prompt notice (if legally permitted), disclose only what is required, and seek protective treatment.

Breach and remedies:
Recipient will promptly notify the Disclosing Party of any unauthorized use or disclosure, take immediate remedial steps, and cooperate in mitigation. The Parties agree monetary damages may be inadequate; the Disclosing Party may seek injunctive relief, specific performance, and recover direct damages, including reasonable attorneys’ fees and costs. The Disclosing Party may suspend or terminate the project. Remedies are cumulative and survive termination.

instruction: Generate a double-stranded DNA consisting of 24 nucleotides in each strand, with an equal number of adenine (A), thymine (T), cytosine (C), and guanine (G) nucleotides. For every 6 nucleotides in the first strand, the first 3 should have a higher proportion of purines (A and G), while the last 3 should have a higher proportion of pyrimidines (C and T). The second strand should be complementary to the first strand, following the base pairing rules (A pairs with T, and C pairs with G).
decomposed_questions: Is the generated sequence a double-stranded DNA?
Does each strand of the generated double-stranded DNA consist of 24 nucleotides?
In the generated double-stranded DNA, is there an equal number of adenine (A), thymine (T), cytosine (C), and guanine (G) nucleotides?
For every set of 6 nucleotides in the first strand of the generated double-stranded DNA, do the first 3 have a higher proportion of purines (A and G)?
For every set of 6 nucleotides in the first strand of the generated double-stranded DNA, do the last 3 have a higher proportion of pyrimidines (C and T)?

Is the second strand of the generated double-stranded DNA complementary to the first strand, adhering to the base pairing rules where adenine (A) pairs with thymine (T), and cytosine (C) pairs with guanine (G)?
output:
First strand (24 nt): AGCACTAGTACTGACGCTGGTACT
Second strand (complement, 24 nt): TCGTGATCATGACTGCGACCATGA

Notes:
- Each strand contains 6 A, 6 T, 6 C, and 6 G.
- In the first strand, each 6-nt block has purine-rich first 3 nt and pyrimidine-rich last 3 nt:
  - Block 1 (1–6): AGC | ACT
  - Block 2 (7–12): AGT | ACT
  - Block 3 (13–18): GAC | GCT
  - Block 4 (19–24): GGT | ACT
- The second strand is the base-pair complement of the first (A↔T, C↔G) at each position.
